title: "Am I Just a Loser?"
author: Ethan Evans
source: Level Up with Ethan Evans (Substack), July 30, 2026
summary: This executive coaching case study follows 'Ram,' a highly qualified consultant who reached the final round of eleven consecutive leadership job searches and finished second every time. The coaching conversation reframes his experience from a character flaw to an addressable behavioral pattern. The key insight is that Ram was suppressing his confidence and executive presence in final-round interviews to seem appropriately humble — but decision-makers read his calibrated presentation as uncertainty. The coach introduces the concept of 'addressable cause' to shift Ram from external blame to targeted self-improvement. The piece argues that for qualified candidates, the margin between being hired and finishing second is often a gap between internal competence and its external expression.
points: Eleven consecutive final-round finishes without an offer is a pattern, not bad luck — patterns have addressable causes.
The coach's framing of 'addressable cause' redirects candidates from self-blame and cosmic explanations to specific, improvable behaviors.
Calibrated humility in final-round interviews can read as uncertainty to decision-makers who are looking for confident, inevitable leaders.
The gap for highly qualified candidates is often between internal certainty and external executive presence, not between actual competence levels.
Blaming cosmic forces is the opposite of identifying and improving a specific behavior — it forecloses the possibility of change.
quotes: I know this sounds dramatic, but... what is wrong with me? Am I unable to get the jobs I want? Am I just a total loser?
Eleven final-round interviews is enough data that I don't think this is random anymore. I think something is going on.
The good news is that if there's a pattern, there's probably an addressable cause.
What he is experiencing is not a character flaw or a permanent condition. Rather it is a behavior to identify and improve.
Ram was highly competent but was presenting himself with insufficient confidence and executive presence in final-round interviews, which decision-makers read as uncertainty.
